chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
title: How 'Confessin' the Blues' and 'Jumpin' the Blues' were made up
summary: The head arrangements for the 1941-42 records were worked out orally, Ramey wrote eight bars and Bird four, building from an old blues theme.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, I take it that after this record of Confessin' the Blues was such a big hit, you had to.

Yeah, that was something that we had just rigged together a few days before we left. In fact, I think Brown joined us in about January and we were down in Wichita and working, and had a few gigs. And went along, the horns, the reeds and the brass, would work out a little thing to do on the tour. Brown knew nothing about music. He just left it up to us.
And the thing began to go over good every place we played. We got down to (unintelligible) everyone was crazy about him.
When you played it I take it that you didn't just play it with the trio. The whole band played it.
The whole band played it. And now this was -- there was never one note written on it. In fact, Bird were and I supposed to have written 'Jumpin' the Blues.' Not one
note was written. Down in Wichita -- I mean, down in New Orleans, and we had to get ready for that 1942 recording date?

And we sat down there and started humming riffs that would fit. (unintelligible). And so I got the first eight bars of that and Bird did the last four. And that was the theme of Jumpin' the Blues. Brown came in and sang, and then as we played and rehearsed it, we made up different riffs that would fit with it, and that became the theme after that. Before that, McShann had an old blues theme that is on that record that you heard in Wichita.
Remember that thing, Bird was playing that mournful background behind something?
Well, that was the theme song. The whole band played that. (Singing.) Now, that might have been the thing that typed us as a blues band.

Because we had to start to using that. But I'll tell you how we got that. We used to -- riding home at night, we used to reminisce about old tunes. There was an old song that somebody sang, that said, (sings) 'well, when my mama's dead and my papa's across the sea,' -- and we used to just enlarge on

that, so this is how this mournful thing got to us. And then as you noticed, sometimes in the solo works the guys would go back to their thing. You listen to the riffs that was played behind it, built off of that.
